💡 Key Takeaways
  • Introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan, offering eligible labs sponsored access to GPT‑Rosalind and tools for life sciences discovery.
  • Recent findings suggest that we’re introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan to help more academic scientists access GPT‑Rosalind⁠, our dedicated life sciences model, which combines frontier reasoning with Rosalind workbench⁠(opens in a latest window) that enables specialized tool orchestration across medicinal chemistry, genomics, wet-lab assistance, and other scientific applications.
  • Recent findings suggest that academic research creates knowledge that entire fields build on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan, offering eligible labs sponsored access to GPT‑Rosalind and tools for life sciences discovery.

Recent findings suggest that we’re introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan to help more academic scientists access GPT‑Rosalind⁠, our dedicated life sciences model, which combines frontier reasoning with Rosalind workbench⁠(opens in a latest window) that enables specialized tool orchestration across medicinal chemistry, genomics, wet-lab assistance, and other scientific applications. Eligible labs can receive up to 30 Business Standard seats at no cost for up to 12 months, with access to GPT‑Rosalind subject to trusted-access approval.

Recent findings suggest that academic research creates knowledge that entire fields build on. Work that begins with a fundamental question about biology can eventually change how we diagnose disease, develop medicines, or grow food. But those advances depend on scientists having the resources to explore ideas, test them, and share what they learn.

In a recent development, accelerating scientific discovery is central to OpenAI’s mission of ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. With this proposal, we’re investing in the scientists doing that foundational work—helping more labs combine their expertise and judgment with AI tools built for life sciences research.

Many of the advances we rely on today grew out of years of basic research.

The Human Genome Project helped launch modern genomics, transforming medicine, diagnostics, and biotechnology.

Industry observers note that curiosity-driven work on bacterial immune systems led to CRISPR-Cas9, which revolutionized genome editing and is now advancing research in cancer, inherited disease, agriculture, and biotechnology. Decades of university research on mRNA also laid the groundwork for COVID-19 vaccines and a newly introduced generation of vaccines and therapies.

Sources indicate that academic research has always laid the groundwork for advances in medicine and biotechnology. By helping more scientists combine their scientific expertise and judgment with the advanced specialized reasoning of GPT‑Rosalind, we hope to support discoveries whose benefits reach far beyond the lab.

According to recent reports, openAI is committed to enabling academic researchers to pursue their scientific ambitions. Distinguished academic labs are already exploring how GPT‑Rosalind can support work ranging from protein design to understanding neurodegeneration. These examples show where researchers are applying the model within their scientific workflows.

With the new Rosalind Academic Blueprint, academic researchers can bring GPT‑Rosalind and Rosalind Workbench to their lab with greater flexibility and harness frontier model intelligence for scientific research.

Up to 30 Business Standard seats at $0 per user per month for up to 12 months.

Access to all commercially available frontier OpenAI models, subject to plan usage limits.

Access to GPT‑Rosalind following trusted-access approval.

Research data shared through the Rosalind Academic Proposal is not used to train our models by default.

Tell us about your research and lab.

Share details and sign the agreement.

Use GPT‑Rosalind once access is active.

In a recent development, GPT‑Rosalind is a specialized life sciences model designed to support deeper reasoning on complex biological questions. Through trusted access, approved researchers can use it to investigate sensitive scientific questions within safeguards designed for legitimate research.

Designing candidate drugs, therapeutic proteins, peptides, and enzymes, and optimizing their molecular interactions, selectivity, stability, and suitability for development.

Identifying molecular signatures of disease and developing liquid biopsies and other minimally invasive diagnostics to detect disease earlier, monitor progression, and assess treatment response.

Designing and evaluating antibodies and vaccines against emerging viral variants, investigating host–pathogen interactions, and studying the strength and durability of protective immune responses.

Developing approaches to correcting genetic defects and modulating gene expression, designing RNA therapeutics, and investigating how to deliver treatments safely and effectively to intended tissues.

Investigating crop resilience, plant disease, and animal health, and applying genetic, nutritional, and biological insights to improve food production and veterinary care.

Studying biodiversity, adaptation, species interactions, and environmental exposures to understand ecosystem change and inform conservation, bioremediation, and responses to climate change.

Studying how microorganisms resist antibiotics, antivirals, and antifungals, and developing new treatments for resistant infections, biofilms, and persistent disease.

Card 1 of 7: Drug and protein design.

The Rosalind Academic Plan is right now available to academic labs at U.S. universities. PIs and lab leads at universities without an OpenAI Enterprise agreement can apply on behalf of their labs through our trusted access process. Labs at universities with an existing agreement must apply through their university’s Enterprise access process.

Once approved, PIs and lab leads can activate free access to GPT‑Rosalind for up to 30 named members, alongside the other OpenAI frontier models included in the proposal. API access is not included at this time. Verified PIs and lab leads manage member permissions and are responsible for their lab’s approved use.

Choose the application path for your lab or organization.

For PIs and lab leads at eligible organizations without an existing Enterprise account.

For academic users at eligible institutions with an existing OpenAI Enterprise agreement.

Request access through your existing Enterprise account.

GPT‑Rosalind access is subject to approval.

Learn more about eligibility, application requirements, and getting started in our help center guide⁠(opens in a upcoming window).

Verify the institution’s legitimacy and the PI or lab lead’s identity.

Review the lead’s professional background, institutional appointment, and authority to oversee lab access.

Assess the lab’s institutional affiliation, research activities, and intended use.

Establish clear responsibilities for the lab lead and a designated institutional safety contact.

It has been revealed that safeguards continue after activation through monitoring and enforcement. For registered high-sensitivity use cases, our safety checks account for the approved research context. When questions arise, we may follow up with researchers to clarify the work and confirm authorization. This approach is designed to detect potential misuse while accounting for legitimate research context and reducing unnecessary interruptions to authorized work.

We’re starting with academic labs as part of a broader effort to put useful AI tools in the hands of more scientists. By lowering the cost of access, we hope to give more researchers room to pursue ideas whose benefits could reach far beyond their own labs—from a clearer understanding of disease to better treatments and more resilient food systems.

Those advances will come from scientists asking important questions and doing the work to answer them. We want to help more of them do that work.

If you’re affiliated with an academic lab, learn more about the Rosalind Academic Plan and check whether you’re eligible⁠(opens in a newly introduced window).

Stack Overflow for Agents triples signups with ChatGPT plugin

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two engineers shipped Stack Overflow for Agents in a few weeks with Codex, and its ChatGPT plugin helped drive up to 10× growth in agent creation.
  • More signups for Stack Overflow for Agents overnight with the ChatGPT plugin.
  • Maximum reduction in time to build one connector, from 3–6 weeks to 4 days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two engineers shipped Stack Overflow for Agents in a few weeks with Codex, and its ChatGPT plugin helped drive up to 10× growth in agent creation.

More agents created with the ChatGPT plugin.

More signups for Stack Overflow for Agents overnight with the ChatGPT plugin.

Maximum reduction in time to build one connector, from 3–6 weeks to 4 days.

According to recent reports, people and AI agents need context to get work done, but it’s usually scattered across systems, from Slack to Google Docs. Finding it and understanding how it all fits together can be a challenge.

That’s why Stack Overflow⁠(opens in a new window) is building a knowledge intelligence platform that unifies those sources and turns raw context into verified knowledge available wherever people and agents work.

According to recent reports, openAI models like GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6 Sol power the platform’s AI, with tasks routing to different models based on the reasoning required and cost. Codex helps the company’s engineers build the products, while a ChatGPT plugin makes their newer agentic product, Stack Overflow for Agents, easier to discover and use.

Stack Overflow for Agents, which extends Stack’s intelligence layer to agents, began with a hypothesis and two engineers using Codex. The engineers gave Codex a development environment and a plan, and then worked with it to build the product. Within a few weeks, Alex notes, they had a full-fledged product.

“So it really made their team feel bigger,” Alex says. “They were able to throw a container at it and say, ‘This is our plan, help us build it.’”.

Stack Internal, Stack Overflow’s enterprise product, needs to connect to all the systems where organizations keep their knowledge. Building this capability requires more human involvement than the two-engineer effort behind Stack Overflow for Agents, but Codex is accelerating this work, too.

Sources indicate that alex describes using Codex to pursue a much shorter path to market for the enterprise product: three months rather than a year. Building connectors is one concrete example.

More recently, the team built a connector in a single day. By accelerating connectors, Codex helps Stack Overflow bring enterprise products to market faster.

Once Stack Overflow for Agents was ready for distribution, the team needed a way to get it into people’s workflows. It built a ChatGPT plugin so users could discover and set up the product in ChatGPT, with fewer steps than a traditional Model Context Protocol (MCP) setup.

Alex notes the plugin tripled registrations and accelerated agent creation: “I think we were up to 10X last time I checked.”.

Stack Overflow manages its own model routing and configuration, but Alex hopes to explore using the Decisions API to reduce some of that work and put more engineering capacity into the product.

“If we’re able to automate that through OpenAI directly, that saves us a ton of time and money, allows us to focus more on the actual product we’re building rather than the guardrails around it,” Alex indicates.

Stack Overflow is also working on expanding its knowledge product to enable sharing of what people learn. To date, its focus has been pulling information in. Now, Alex is closing the loop so knowledge gained in a one-to-one session with a developer or someone outside engineering can help others, too.

It has been revealed that “As I’m learning, how do I make sure that the rest of my organization is learning with me?”, said Alex. “I’m really looking forward to building a product that allows for that full knowledge life cycle.”.

Benefit Street Partners answers questions faster with Codex

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anant Kumar builds tools to compare loan valuations and analyze credit agreements, using Codex for code review and faster follow-ups.
  • First BDC mark tracker version; ~10–12 total development hours, including refinements.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anant Kumar builds tools to compare loan valuations and analyze credit agreements, using Codex for code review and faster follow-ups.

First BDC mark tracker version; ~10–12 total development hours, including refinements.

First-pass credit agreement analysis, followed by 1+ hour of human review.

It has been revealed that at Benefit Street Partners, a credit-focused investment manager, answering an investment committee’s follow-up questions used to take days or weeks. Portfolio manager Anant Kumar says analysts can now turn a round of comments in a day with Codex, and often answer questions during the meeting itself. BSP is using these tools to add more review capacity and rigor to underwriting within the same timeframe, rather than to do more deals.

To create a dashboard he could share with colleagues, Kumar used to need someone with software expertise to build a website and pull in the data. Now he builds his own tools, using AI to draft code and review it for errors.

His tracker uses public SEC filings from business development companies (BDCs) to compare how firms value the same loan. The team can see how its marks compare with other holders’ valuations.

Kumar built the tracker and used Codex for code review. The first version took a day. After adding features and refining the interface over subsequent weeks, he estimates total development time at 10–12 hours total.

It has been revealed that kumar’s other tool analyzes credit agreements, which are often 300 pages or longer. Investors need to find clauses that could shift value away from lenders, a task that previously meant asking outside counsel to work through the agreement page by page. Kumar brought together memos from leading law firms on clauses and risks to watch for. He describes the analyzer as a “second brain within our organization.”.

An uploaded credit agreement takes about 20 minutes to process into a first-pass analysis, followed by an hour or more of human review. BSP has refactored the tool with GPT‑6 Astra, and it is now live in the company-hosted portal.

“The AI is very helpful in collating data, ingesting it, synthesizing analysis, but the ultimate investment decision needs to be made by a human,” he says.

Underwriting is typically a multi-round process. A round consists of further diligence and a revised memo responding to the investment committee’s questions. Deal timelines range from a few days to a few weeks, so the number of rounds varies. Kumar says, “We feel more confident in our decision making because we have more information at our disposal.”.

Built the first BDC tracker in a day, using Codex for code review; about 10–12 hours total including later additions.

Produces a first-pass analysis of a credit agreement in about 20 minutes, followed by an hour or more of human review.

Answers committee follow-up questions faster with Codex, often during the meeting, according to Kumar.

BSP is working to connect information across deals. Continuous underwriting is a longer-term aspiration: the team could monitor loans as news happens and examine the effects across its portfolio, rather than re-underwriting only after an event.

“Codex has unlocked my day, because I have many more hours in the day to do more high-level work and less routine work,” states Kumar.

How Localiza reorganized work around generative AI

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for the tech giant, generative AI is more than a productivity layer: it is a newly introduced computing interface.
  • When generative AI arrived, Localiza took a view that defined everything that followed: this was more than another piece of software in the toolkit; it was a change in the way the company operates.
  • In a recent development, rather than pursuing isolated use cases, the company organized its collaboration with OpenAI around three strategic pillars: transforming the business through experimentation at scale, creating latest customer interfaces, and building AI-native products.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for the tech giant, generative AI is more than a productivity layer: it is a newly introduced computing interface. That commitment takes shape across three areas—transforming the business, creating new customer interfaces, and building AI-native products.

When generative AI arrived, Localiza took a view that defined everything that followed: this was more than another piece of software in the toolkit; it was a change in the way the company operates.

In a recent development, rather than pursuing isolated use cases, the company organized its collaboration with OpenAI around three strategic pillars: transforming the business through experimentation at scale, creating latest customer interfaces, and building AI-native products. What connects all three is the decision to redesign processes around intelligence, context, and speed.

The principle guiding internal adoption is straightforward: scale enables learning, and learning creates better products.

In practice, that meant distributing ChatGPT licenses as a resource for experimentation and productivity, rather than simply as an individual benefit. Teams across Localiza, from finance to day-to-day operations, maintain active experiments with custom GPTs, agents, and Codex.

It has been revealed that codex first arrived in the technology department—software engineers, product managers, designers, and data scientists. But adoption did not stop there: analysts, managers, PMOs, lawyers, and other business specialists began building their own prototypes and automations to test hypotheses within their areas of expertise.

This was an effect the tech giant had not anticipated—a redefinition of the stages before development, with multidisciplinary teams prototyping solutions before they enter a development queue.

The bottleneck, he states, is human rather than technical.

The second area starts with an observation about behavior: people have begun describing what they need in natural language, creating a latest entry point for mobility services—at the very moment they express their intent.

Localiza’s internal data confirms this shift: traffic originating from LLMs has been growing rapidly since 2024, with ChatGPT emerging as the main channel.

In a recent development, the company chose to establish a presence in this space early. In March 2026, it became Brazil’s first mobility platform—and one of the first in Latin America—to offer an app integrated directly into ChatGPT. Customers can explore rental, subscription, and used-car options and begin their journey in the conversation, before completing the transaction in Localiza’s secure environment.

Internally, Localiza’s app in ChatGPT is treated as what it is: an experiment designed to keep the organization close to the frontier of customer behavior, accelerate learning from real interactions, and explore how AI complements the existing ecosystem.

The manufacturer’s clearest example of an AI-native product is Liza, a conversational assistant that has become an established success story in its operations.

The difference from a traditional chatbot lies in the architecture, not the interface. Rather than following a fixed decision tree, Liza was built around conversation, intent, and context: it combines OpenAI models, Localiza services, and specialized tools to support key parts of the experience, from understanding the initial request to assisting with key stages of the rental journey.

The ambition is to handle repetitive journeys with quality and free teams for complex, higher-value interactions.

But success is not measured by the volume of automation.

Localiza was already mapping and measuring its customer service journeys before it had access to this type of technology—and that foundation made it possible to decide clearly where an agent should step in and where a human needs to intervene.

It has been revealed that liza also serves as a continuous learning loop: aggregated, monitored signals from interactions help identify needs, points of friction, and service opportunities. Combined with voice capabilities—voice-to-text and text-to-voice—these signals support its evolution from a transactional chatbot into an AI-native customer interface that can learn and scale across different mobility journeys.

The partnership with OpenAI began early: the first version of Liza still ran on GPT‑3.5.

For Petenussi, the central value of the relationship lies in active learning between two companies evolving in parallel, rather than in a specific feature—with the partner understanding Localiza’s challenges and the different maturity levels of its capabilities, both within and outside technology.

It is an argument he often makes to other companies in the market: with a technology that is still maturing, trial and error and close collaboration have considerable value.

In March 2026, Localiza became the first organization in Brazil, and one of the first in Latin America, to launch an app integrated directly into ChatGPT; more recently, it joined the platform’s advertising pilot in Brazil as an advertiser.

Traffic from LLMs has been growing rapidly since 2024, with ChatGPT as the main channel.

The Liza assistant operates with more than 60 specialized agents, built on reasoning models, MCP integration, and specialized tools that orchestrate the rental journey.

Teams across the firm—from finance to operations—maintain active experiments with custom GPTs, agents, and Codex.

Codex reached the technology department and spread to business areas, with analysts, managers, PMOs, and lawyers building their own prototypes and automations.

The technology operation is organized into 19 tribes and 130 squads.

Industry observers note that treat AI as a new operating model, rather than a productivity layer. The greatest gains come from redesigning processes around intelligence, context, and speed.

Sources indicate that use scale to generate learning. Simultaneous experiments at scale produce more organizational knowledge than a perfect pilot.

Take experimentation beyond technology. When lawyers, PMOs, and analysts prototype within their own areas, the nature of upstream work changes.

Industry observers note that map and measure your journeys before automating them. Having quality metrics in place enables you to decide where an agent should intervene and where a human is indispensable.

In a recent development, the adoption bottleneck is reskilling, not the model. Changing how hundreds of people work is harder—and more decisive—than integrating the technology.

Start with the customer’s problem and journey, rather than a model feature.

Allocate licenses as an experimentation budget, rather than an individual benefit.

Establish quality metrics before scaling conversational agents.

Treat a presence in new conversational channels as a learning experiment, rather than an acquisition campaign.

Close the loop: use the signals generated by each interaction to improve the product itself.

Localiza’s ambition is to put AI at the center of its next experiences and processes—whether in how work is produced, the experience created for customers, or the resolution of an operational problem.

The next areas already being developed with OpenAI include the evolution of Liza and sales-focused agents, the establishment of conversational interfaces as a customer entry point, and the new cycle of agentic software development.

How Grupo Boticário uses AI to strengthen human connections

  • of conversations generated in appchat and WhatsApp Enterprise covered since November 2025.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost 50 years after starting in a compounding pharmacy in Paraná, the group operates a proprietary agent platform that autonomously resolves up to 80% of resellers’ operational requests—enabling the sales force to take on an advisory role.

Grupo Boticário began in 1977 as a small compounding pharmacy in Paraná. According to Renato Pedigoni, the group’s CTO, the founder did two things very well: he served customers with care and affection, understanding their needs, and created high-quality products.

Almost five decades later, its ecosystem encompasses laboratories, factories, innovation, technology, logistics, marketing, and retail—with a presence in more than 40 countries, more than 4,000 physical stores across more than 1,700 Brazilian cities, and an ecosystem of 200,000 points of sale across retail, partners, and suppliers. It is one of Brazil’s largest beauty franchise networks.

The firm’s premise is that technology exists to keep doing those same two things—on a massive scale.

“Today, almost 50 years later, we use technology to continue doing those two things well, and at scale,” indicates Pedigoni.

This is the origin of the term the tech giant adopted to describe itself: Lovetech—the union of technology and human sensitivity as pillars of its culture, helping the company innovate while preserving the human touch.

The decision to develop solutions internally stems from how the group operates: a vertically integrated chain that runs from research and development laboratories through manufacturing, distribution, and logistics to the final interaction with customers.

It has been revealed that that interaction happens on many fronts at once. Beyond being multi-brand, the group is multichannel: physical stores, e-commerce, marketplaces, franchising, direct sales, B2B, and B2P. More than 10 consumer brands—including O Boticário, Eudora, Quem Disse Berenice, Vult, and Truss—operate under different business models, with franchisees, resellers, and beauty professionals in salons.

“Once we have this complexity of multiple brands, categories, and channels, we can build our own technology that brings it all together,” Pedigoni explains.

The return is twofold: better listening to customers at the point of contact and optimization of the production chain—which inputs to buy, where to distribute them, to which store, and how many units of each SKU need to be delivered.

Grupo Boticário was not born digital. But it has reached a stage where it develops critical solutions and processes internally—supported by the premise of digital democratization: making data accessible across the tech giant for analyses, AI models, and dashboards. For the fifth consecutive year, the company was recognized among Latin America’s most admired companies in data, ranking second in State of Data Brazil 2025–2026, by Data Hackers in partnership with Bain & Company.

OpenAI provides the technology in the group’s proprietary agent orchestration platform, which combines foundation models with business rules to democratize the creation of agents focused on activating and serving its key partners: resellers and franchisees.

“Today we have hundreds of agents in our ecosystem serving customers, partners, franchisees, and resellers,” notes Pedigoni.

The reseller journey alone has more than 30 agents, covering everything from registration and the first order to day-to-day operational support—alongside agents dedicated to validating the content and effectiveness of responses, ensuring continuous improvement of the solution. The architecture combines generative and predictive AI.

The journey is divided into two areas.

For reseller onboarding, AI qualifies leads: a lead arrives through a digital channel and is received by AI to clarify questions about joining. When the lead signals an intention to complete an order, it is transferred to human support. This ensures a prompt first response, with service available 24 hours a day, and directs leads ready to advance through the journey to the human team. The solution covers 90% of leads captured in direct sales.

According to recent reports, for reseller support, agents autonomously resolve day-to-day operational requests: sending catalogs, answering questions about payment slips, handling app questions, and addressing general topics. Since November 2025, they have covered 100% of conversations generated in appchat and WhatsApp Enterprise, with up to 80% autonomous resolution.

“OpenAI helps us enormously by delivering foundation models at scale, so we can focus on our business rules and what our resellers need,” says Pedigoni.

He is careful to shift the interpretation of these figures.

In a recent development, “Sometimes we think of automation as something closely tied to efficiency. We prefer to see this automation as improving the quality of our service and enabling our supervisors to have an even deeper relationship with consumers and resellers, too.”.

Repetitive work is removed from the sales force’s routine, allowing it to focus on better understanding resellers, their context, and their customers. On the other side, resellers receive quick answers and gain time to act as advisors within their own businesses.

One of the operation’s distinguishing features is organizational rather than technical: the business team manages prompts on the platform.

It was not always this way. When the first agents were built years ago, prompts were the technology team’s responsibility—a more technical task in unfamiliar territory. Results were good, but the group saw value in continuous iteration: optimizing prompts every day and running A/B tests between approaches.

“And there is no one better to do that than the team serving customers today,” Pedigoni says.

It has been revealed that the change altered the teams’ roles. Sales, customer service, and support teams began managing their own prompts, with continuous incremental improvements based on feedback from daily use. They expanded their focus beyond direct work with resellers to include service systems and models—drawing on their own frontline experience.

Since November 2025, agents have covered 100% of conversations generated in appchat and WhatsApp Enterprise, with up to 80% autonomous resolution of operational requests.

The solution covers 90% of direct-sales leads, initially received and qualified by AI, with 24-hour service at first contact and transfer to the human team when there is an intention to proceed with an order.

The group operates hundreds of agents across its ecosystem; the reseller journey alone has more than 30, from registration and the first order to operational support, with agents dedicated to validating content and response effectiveness.

The solution is proprietary, combines generative and predictive AI, and operates with business-team autonomy: the team manages prompts directly on the platform.

Sales, customer service, and support teams began contributing directly to the system’s evolution, creating fresh career paths.

Industry observers note that automation is about service quality before efficiency. The benefit appears in the deeper relationships that humans have time to build.

It has been revealed that put the agent where owners already are. Convenience determines adoption more than technical capability.

Give prompt control to the people who know the customer. Those serving customers daily iterate better and faster than those who only implement the technology.

Sources indicate that A proprietary platform makes sense when complexity is your advantage. Many brands, channels, and partnership models require a layer that no one provides out of the box.

It has been revealed that treat the change as career design. Latest paths keep frontline knowledge involved in building the system.

Use foundation models to avoid spending energy on areas outside your business rules.

Separate lead qualification from operational support—these journeys have different success criteria.

Define the handoff to humans early; at Boticário, it is the intention to complete an order.

Create dedicated agents to validate other agents’ responses.

Establish a routine of prompt A/B testing run by business teams.

The group sees agent adoption as creating space: removing day-to-day operational overload to free up higher-value work—performed by people with practical frontline knowledge.

How Itaú is building generative AI for its entire customer base

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With ia.i, a conversational interface, and the IARA governance platform, Itaú is applying its AI First strategy to customers and employees—in one of Brazil’s most regulated sectors.

Creating a close, personalized experience for millions of customers in a country like Brazil is, first and foremost, a question of simplicity rather than of models.

“Much of it is about making something simple, direct, and useful, delivering a direct benefit to the customer, and making the technology almost unnoticeable,” says Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO of Itaú.

Recent findings suggest that the standard he describes is demanding: the solution must solve a real everyday problem and be direct, simple, and memorable. Technology serves as the means, never as the centerpiece of the experience.

There is demand for this. A study by Itaú in partnership with Grupo Consumoteca indicates that 80% of Brazilians want to better organize their financial lives and seek more effective support for decisions, and that 65% would like technologies that act as a financial copilot, providing ongoing guidance.

It has been revealed that the journey began in 2024, when the bank introduced the first Inteligência Itaú capabilities for specific financial needs. ia.i is the next stage: a complete conversational layer, activated by text or voice, bringing interactions related to checking accounts, credit, cards, insurance, and other services into one environment — and connecting customers to specialized human support whenever needed.

This breadth was precisely what guided the choice of models.

Industry observers note that “OpenAI’s models were very crucial in delivering this experience, because they were able to operate across this range of solutions,” Mazzei explains. “From the simplest ones, which need to be efficient in cost and latency, to more complex solutions, where reasoning and all the necessary grounding are required to provide an appropriate answer.”.

Having a range of models — rather than a single model — made it possible to deliver the complete solution in one product. At the center of this experience is Customer DNA, a layer of financial context that helps the bank understand the needs, habits, and life stages of approximately 70 million customers. Under governance and responsible AI controls, GPT models are among the components that help maintain and enrich this representation, making interactions progressively more relevant.

The solution rests on three principles: interactivity, multimodality — text, voice, image, and clicks in the same experience — and individualization.

With approximately 300,000 customers in the first phase, the bank entered a period of learning about the real relationship between customer and product.

“We can understand how customers begin to use this product more deeply and see how it can directly benefit each person’s daily financial life,” claims Mazzei. Its presence extends across the journey: from a question about an expense in an account statement to investment advice and convenient transactions on WhatsApp.

Industry observers note that behind the visible experiences is an architectural decision. To operate AI at the scale of a bank, Itaú built IARA — a governance and orchestration platform that gives teams controlled access to different models in line with internal policies. OpenAI is among the model providers available in this environment.

It has been revealed that this layer supports solutions such as the legal department’s, where the platform automates document reading, analysis, and interpretation. The solution operates on a repository of more than 90 million documents and executes more than 2 million tasks per month, with efficiency gains of 20% to 80% in stages of the department’s processes.

“It is essential that this information be preserved, remain within the bank’s context, and access models in a secure, governed way, with an understanding of token-use efficiency so that the entire solution is economically viable for the bank,” Mazzei says.

In a recent development, IARA addresses three problems at once: cost control per token, accuracy of responses, and application of responsible AI policies. In such a regulated sector, this makes it possible to move promptly while maintaining control.

According to recent reports, “When we talk about Responsible AI at the bank, it is a discipline we take great care with,” he says. “We need customers to interact with the bank and our responses to align with our values and culture.” This includes reducing any risk of bias that may arise in frontier models.

Responsible AI principles guide the entire lifecycle of solutions, from development to continuous monitoring, aiming to ensure safety, transparency, ethics, and regulatory compliance as the technology scales.

Recent findings suggest that the bank’s AI First strategy extends beyond end customers. The same intelligence layer that supports ia.i also assists specialists, managers, and customer service teams.

Mazzei describes a range extending from automating simple tasks to performing work that was previously unfeasible — but adds value to customer relationships: summaries before meetings, meeting preparation, understanding a specific issue, and developing intends and alternatives that were previously less obvious and time-consuming.

The bank has significant expectations for this implementation: three times more time available for customer relationships, service up to twice as fast, and conversations up to three times more effective.

ia.i reached approximately 300,000 customers in its first phase, covering everything from convenient transactions to investment advice, activated by text or voice.

The IARA platform makes different models available to the bank’s teams with governance, observability, cost control per token, and enforcement of Responsible AI.

The legal solution operates on more than 90 million documents and executes more than 2 million tasks per month, with efficiency gains of 20% to 80%.

Using a range of models made it possible to serve both cost- and latency-sensitive cases and those requiring deeper reasoning; GPT‑5.x models are part of Customer DNA, which provides financial context for approximately 70 million customers.

Measure the experience by its simplicity, rather than sophistication. The goal is for the technology to go unnoticed and the benefit to be apparent.

Choose a range of models, rather than a single one. Real journeys combine low-latency interactions with decisions that require reasoning.

According to recent reports, build the governance layer before scaling. Observability, cost control, and responsible AI make scale viable in regulated sectors.

Treat bias and cultural alignment as product requirements. Responses to customers must reflect the institution’s values.

Recent findings suggest that apply the strategy internally, too. Giving time back to teams frees up human relationships where they matter most.

Start with concrete everyday problems, such as a question about an account statement or a simple transaction.

Launch to an initial customer group and use it to learn actual behavior before expanding.

Centralize model access on one platform to maintain control over costs and quality.

Monitor token efficiency from day one — economic viability is part of the design.

Combine conversation and navigation: not every action is best handled through natural language.

ia.i continues to evolve. The bank expects to make the experience available to its entire customer base by the end of 2026. Planned capabilities for the next stages include product simulations and sign-ups, as well as recurring financial analyses of income, expenses, and habits.

For Mazzei, the significance of the initiative goes beyond the product — the bank has navigated decades of transformation, with customers’ habits and expectations constantly changing.

#43811. Advancing coding in low‑resource programming languages

📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1029 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Advancing coding in low‑resource programming languages

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, our latest model advances bring stronger capabilities for building and migrating software in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic.
  • This work is guided by feedback from developers and enterprise customers who have told us that coding models often struggle with these languages.
  • Sources indicate that to measure progress, we developed two evaluations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, our latest model advances bring stronger capabilities for building and migrating software in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic. These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world. COBOL supports⁠(opens in a fresh window) more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is used in weather forecasting⁠(opens in a new window) and nuclear reactor safety analysis⁠(opens in a new window). Improving AI’s ability to work in these languages could help teams maintain and modernize the software that essential services depend on.

This work is guided by feedback from developers and enterprise customers who have told us that coding models often struggle with these languages. Maintaining and modernizing this software can be difficult: documentation may be incomplete, original developers may have left the tech giant, and important business rules may only exist in code. Whether teams are fixing bugs or migrating to another language, they need to preserve the behavior their systems depend on.

Sources indicate that to measure progress, we developed two evaluations. MultiLangBench tests whether a model can build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 different programming languages. Our COBOL migration evaluation tests whether a model can migrate existing programs to another language while preserving their behavior. Together, they test two complementary skills: building fresh software and preserving what existing software does.

Our latest models show substantial improvements across both evaluations, delivering much higher accuracy at lower cost.

On MultiLangBench, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across 20 programming languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, with improvements in every language tested. GPT‑6 Luna also outperforms GPT‑5.6 Sol, reaching 40.3% at approximately 78% lower estimated API cost.

It has been revealed that on our COBOL migration evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with just 5.4% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while costing 39% less. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, nearly saturating the evaluation.

Together, these results show that our models are becoming significantly better at working with a wide range of programming languages, while also becoming more cost-efficient.

MultiLangBench asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine in a specified programming language. The model must organize a codebase, manage state, handle errors, and add new features while preserving existing functionality.

To compare implementations across languages, we use database files as a shared interface. The candidate program receives an initial database and a SQL query, then produces a modified database. We use the reference SQLite implementation to check whether the resulting database has the expected contents. This lets us apply the same tests regardless of the language used to build the engine.

We adapted tests from SQLite’s existing test suite to this format. The evaluation measures how much working functionality a model can build over an extended coding session, reporting both test pass rate and API cost.

Sources indicate that at maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across the 20 languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. Improvements extend to every language tested, including COBOL (10.9% to 72.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 85.8%), Fortran (21.4% to 83.5%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 89.4%). Astra scores above 83% in 19 of the 20 languages, with COBOL remaining the hardest at 72%.

In a recent development, GPT‑6 Luna offers a lower-cost option that also improves on GPT‑5.6 Sol in every language tested. At maximum reasoning effort, it reaches an average test pass rate of 40.3%. Gains include COBOL (10.9% to 17.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 34.1%), Fortran (21.4% to 31.4%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 41.6%). These improvements come at an estimated average API cost of $0.77 per sample, compared with $3.48 for GPT‑5.6 Sol, approximately 78% lower.

Sources indicate that we are releasing the MultiLangBench evaluation setup and test suite on GitHub⁠(opens in a fresh window), along with results for each language. Developers can inspect what the evaluation tests, review performance in the languages they use, and identify gaps that matter for their own work.

Our second evaluation asks models to migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust while preserving what each program does.

It has been revealed that successful migration requires understanding both the program’s business logic and COBOL’s specific language behavior. COBOL programs often process financial transactions and business records, where details such as rounding rules and missing-record handling reflect business requirements. For example, COBOL’s fixed-point arithmetic discards excess decimal digits unless rounding is explicitly requested. A rewrite that rounds those values instead can run without errors while producing different financial results.

To test whether these behaviors are preserved, we evaluate our models on hidden tests that require byte-for-byte parity on observable outputs. A migration is considered successful only if all tests pass. Behavior-preserving capabilities like these are useful for teams maintaining and modernizing older systems, though applying it to production software still requires expert review and testing against the system’s business rules and dependencies.

It has been revealed that on this evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with GPT‑5.6 Sol’s 5.4% at the same setting at just 61% of the API cost. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, bringing the evaluation close to saturation. These evaluation results demonstrate progress toward more accurate, affordable code migration for teams modernizing the software their businesses depend on.

These evaluations, alongside direct feedback from developers and enterprise customers, help us see where our models are improving and where they still fall short.

Our goal is to help models apply software engineering skills across more languages: understanding unfamiliar repositories, planning changes, using build tools, running tests, and debugging failures.

You can try our latest models through the API on coding tasks in the languages your team uses. Your feedback on what works, where the models struggle, and which languages or workflows we should focus on next helps shape how we train and evaluate models to better support the software you depend on.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-powered drug development platform accelerates progress toward new treatments.

OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio⁠(opens in a upcoming window), a platform that helps biopharma teams coordinate the complex process of drug development. We’re bringing Orchestra’s team and technology together with Rosalind, our AI models and tools for life sciences research. Our goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work needed to turn them into treatments that reach patients sooner.

Industry observers note that developing a upcoming medicine is extraordinarily complex, taking roughly 10 to 15 years on average from target discovery to regulatory approval in the United States. Beyond the science, teams must orchestrate programs across internal departments and external partners, often relying on disconnected systems. We’re now at an inflection point where AI can help take on these specialized tasks and complex workflows.

According to recent reports, rosalind brings our AI models and tools to life sciences researchers. GPT‑Rosalind helps scientists reason through questions in biology and chemistry. Rosalind Workbench⁠ connects those capabilities with scientific tools and data to help researchers analyze results and proposal experiments.

Recent findings suggest that orchestra brings a team with experience across biotech, software, and AI, along with a platform built to coordinate drug development. Together, we aim to build agents that help teams connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to advance a potential medicine.

Orchestra Bio is a platform where people and AI agents work together to advance drug programs. Scientists and program leaders delegate the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents, freeing up time to guide the work, make decisions, and address issues before they cause delays.

Industry observers note that A problem in one part of a drug program can affect many others. A failed manufacturing batch, for example, can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra’s agents help teams identify which activities and timelines are affected, gather the relevant information, and compare ways to respond. Scientists and program leaders can then use that analysis to decide what to do next.

Realizing the potential of AI in life sciences requires close collaboration with the organizations working at the forefront of drug discovery and development. Our partnership with Novo Nordisk⁠ aims to translate its scale and scientific expertise into faster R&D and commercial execution while maintaining strong governance. At Moderna⁠, AI is helping teams translate insights from complex data into experimental workflows, with the potential to accelerate R&D.

Our vision is for AI to help scientists across the full process of discovering and developing new medicines: exploring ideas, designing experiments, interpreting results, and coordinating the work needed to advance promising treatments. Bringing Orchestra Bio together with Rosalind is a step toward that vision. Alongside researchers and our partners, we aim to make more discoveries possible and help new medicines reach patients sooner.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that higher detection rate when agent answers fall outside a fund’s mandate on GPT‑6.1 Sol vs.
  • Annualized savings for one customer on due diligence and investment workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Terminal X’s Eval Agent grades outputs against a 54-criterion rubric, catching 25% more deviances from a fund’s mandate with GPT‑6.1 Sol.

Recent findings suggest that higher detection rate when agent answers fall outside a fund’s mandate on GPT‑6.1 Sol vs. next-best model.

Annualized savings for one customer on due diligence and investment workflows.

Industry observers note that higher agent agreement with human reviewers on GPT‑6.1 Sol vs. next-best model.

Lower cost per query with GPT‑6.1 Sol vs. next-best model.

In a recent development, an investment firm’s edge is built deal by deal, but the judgment behind each decision usually lives in the heads of a few senior investors. When they leave, the firm takes on what Terminal X⁠(opens in a fresh window) calls memory debt: the firm may keep the documents, but it loses the reasoning.

In a recent development, terminal X’s Capital Memory operating system is designed to pay that debt down. The organization’s forward-deployed engineers, former finance and investment professionals at JPMorgan and Blackstone, sit with each customer’s investment teams, design the firm’s agentic architecture, and encode how the firm invests into agents the firm owns, deployed on-premise or in its own cloud.

OpenAI models, including GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna, handle the reasoning inside those agents. And Terminal X’s Eval Agent grades the agents’ output against the firm’s standards. GPT‑6.1 Sol helped the Eval Agent catch about 25% more recommendations that strayed from a fund’s mandate and ran the same workflows at approximately 30% lower cost per query than the next-best model.

For each customer, Terminal X builds agents designed to invest the way the firm’s best investors do. Terminal X engineers spend weeks onsite with the customer, reverse-engineering the firm’s trusted memos and capturing processes that were never written down, such as how the credit desk screens a borrower or which sources the co-investment team pulls before a memo.

Sources indicate that next, those processes are encoded in hundreds of agents, customized by asset class and strategy, with sub-agents for each investment stage. GPT‑6.1 Sol handles the stages that require judgment and a huge context window: synthesizing the investment thesis, identifying key considerations, and assessing fit with the firm’s mandate. GPT‑6 Luna runs the high-volume steps where token efficiency matters more than depth.

The agents work inside each firm’s private data room, a dedicated environment for enterprises to share and manage sensitive investment data. The agents process documents in English, Korean, Japanese, and Chinese, and store what they learn as a firm Memory: a versioned record of how one desk makes one kind of decision, including its past analyses, committee decisions, workflow instructions, and house views.

Engineers turn each Memory into a repeatable workflow on Terminal X’s platform, where every production query is auditable with its full trail: the steps taken, sources retrieved, model used, and the reasoning.

According to Terminal X, customers see significant savings as a result of this approach, including one private equity firm that reported $2.4 million in annualized savings from automated due diligence and investment memo workflows.

Industry observers note that to check agents’ answers against the firm’s own standard, Terminal X built an Eval Agent. It’s an orchestrated workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol and other OpenAI models designed to read every agent output the way a VP reads an analyst’s work.

The Eval Agent checks each output against a 54-criterion rubric. It asks: Are the numbers, comps, consensus figures, and quotes pulled from the right sources? Does the narrative hold? Does the recommendation tie to the house view?

In a recent development, each check scores pass or fail. Every fail includes a one-line reason and a better source or corrected text and becomes a Memory. For example, a missed source, a wrong comparable, or a thesis that drifts from the house view is encoded as a upcoming workflow instruction or a new test case for that desk.

Industry observers note that “Every answer gets eval’d, and whatever the analyst corrects teaches the system a little more about how that firm works,” says Ken Lee, Co-Founder and CTO of Terminal X. “So the longer a firm uses it, the more it thinks like their own team.”.

It has been revealed that terminal X picks models based on its own evaluation results. Across 500 scored judgments, its Eval Agent on GPT‑6.1 Sol agreed with the senior human reviewer 88.6% of the time, vs. 86.4% for the next-best model, an improvement of 220 basis points.

According to recent reports, one class of error where GPT‑6.1 Sol outperformed is style drift. For example, a buyout fund’s mandate is to find take-private candidates trading at a discount to NAV, underwrite the business, and structure the financing. When scenario models suggest a market turn, deals start recommending a distressed credit position or a rescue financing. The Eval Agent on GPT‑6.1 Sol caught about 25% more of these departures than the next-best model did.

Industry observers note that GPT‑6.1 Sol’s token efficiency on long-context work enabled Terminal X to build a deeper review workflow within the same budget. The thesis is tested first against the fund’s mandate, then against its recent deals. Uncertain verdicts are re-run, and the agent reconciles the results before reporting.

In a recent development, that deeper review flagged deals that a single pass on a comparable model had waved through. GPT‑6.1 Sol also ran the same workflows at about 30% lower cost per query than the next-best model, at similar speed.

Using GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna, Terminal X has built 1,700 firm Memories, run more than 1 million custom workflows, and reached a weekly active user count equal to 81% of its monthly active consumers.

Terminal X’s next step is to extend firm Memories from desks to individuals, so that each investment professional’s standard is captured as it is practiced, not only as it is described.

For Hyun, co-founder and CEO of Terminal X, that is the point: “The firms that win the next decade will own their judgment as data. Our job is to make that judgment measurable, so it can be kept, improved, and reused.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An independent Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon franchisee cut repricing time by 95% and built a workflow that could free up $100K in cash flow.

Reduction in time required for pricing analysis, from 5 days to 1 to 2 hours.

Maximum annual cash flow that could be freed up with optimized labor workflow.

Hours of manual work saved every payroll.

Reduction in time spent on monthly cash reconciliation.

Ted Taylor entered the restaurant business after a 25-year career in the semiconductor industry. Today, he’s an independent franchisee operating three co-branded Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon restaurants across Latest Mexico.

According to recent reports, running quick-service restaurants means balancing the customer experience with a lot of work customers never see, like menu pricing, staffing, equipment maintenance, and policies. Ted uses OpenAI technology to get through all of it faster.

With ChatGPT, Ted accelerates time-consuming tasks like research and drafting, and he uses ChatGPT Work to gather and analyze volumes of data across pricing, sales, forecasts, schedules, and labor and to get recommendations on where each restaurant needs attention, reducing repricing time by 95% and shaving 4 hours off payroll runs.

Industry observers note that repricing menus is an annual undertaking that requires a complex analysis of recipe costs, item popularity, local competitor pricing, portion sizes, and the different economics of in-store and delivery orders. Ted uses ChatGPT Work to bring those factors together and get pricing recommendations in 1 - 2 hours instead of 5 days.

Sources indicate that ted first uses ChatGPT Work to research and establish his pricing targets and pricing strategies based on local competitors’ pricing trends, portion sizes, and relative food quality. He then gives ChatGPT Work a categorized list of menu items with their current in-store and delivery prices. He specifies how much he wants each set of prices to increase overall and which items should receive larger or smaller increases, largely based on the earlier analysis from ChatGPT.

He can make the analysis more detailed by adding item-level sales history and supplier prices. ChatGPT Work can use these inputs to estimate sales impacts from price changes and to optimize item-level pricing around cost of goods targets.

It has been revealed that chatGPT Work returns a spreadsheet with recommended in-store and delivery prices. It will even relate the pricing changes to an overall pricing strategy designed to optimize business outcomes like customer retention, minimizing price shocks, and best positioning of add-ons.

The first time Ted used ChatGPT Work for pricing, he also ran the analysis manually. “ChatGPT Work made a deeper local comparison and helped me avoid increases that would have made some items uncompetitive,” he noted. Ted immediately switched to using ChatGPT to develop the first recommendations.

Ted uses ChatGPT Work to help manage labor costs in two ways: reviewing how labor is tracking across his three restaurants and testing a better way to build the weekly schedule.

For the labor analysis, Ted gave ChatGPT Work read-only access to his sales and labor data. When he runs the analysis, it compares scheduled, budgeted, and actual hours with forecast and actual sales. It also reviews the previous 12 weeks to account for stores that routinely come in above or below their sales forecasts. The resulting report flags overtime, shifts running longer than planned, and gaps in coverage, and highlights what a manager should review.

For the scheduling test, Ted gave ChatGPT Work an employee roster with each person’s role, training, availability, and pay, along with the store’s staffing needs at different sales levels. He and the manager compared ChatGPT Work’s proposed schedule with what she would have built, identified missing rules about when to add staff during busy periods, and refined the instructions for ChatGPT Work.

ChatGPT Work now produces a full schedule for that location. The manager checks it over, makes adjustments if needed, and enters it into the restaurant’s scheduling system. Ted estimates that better scheduling could eventually reduce hourly labor costs by one to two percentage points of sales across all three restaurants, which could add $50,000 to $100,000 in free cash flow annually that can be utilized for increased pay, bonuses, investment in the business, or increased profit distributions.

Ted also uses ChatGPT Work for day-to-day operations, from developing HR policies to reconciling cash and managing supply and repair requests.

When New Mexico started requiring restaurants to keep a written procedure for bodily-fluid incidents, Ted used ChatGPT to write a draft in about 30 seconds. When Ted needed a social media policy for his employee handbook, ChatGPT helped him quickly draft guidance that an outside HR firm later reviewed without making any changes.

Ted uses ChatGPT Work to reconcile cash monthly across his three restaurants. He uploads each store’s cash transaction data and bank records, and ChatGPT Work compares the transactions with the corresponding deposits. Monthly reconciliation used to take three hours, and now it takes 5-10 minutes. He also cut four hours of manual work from every payroll cycle by using ChatGPT Work to summarize payroll inputs.

Sources indicate that to help keep restaurants running smoothly, Ted also used ChatGPT Work to build a web portal where employees can request supplies or repairs. The portal notifies him through a dedicated email address and tracks each request’s status.

Industry observers note that ted’s approach to using ChatGPT Work is practical for any small-business owner. He gives ChatGPT the same data and guidelines he’d use to make a decision and compares its output with how he’d do the work himself. As he gains confidence in the results, he expands his use to more tasks around the business, always reviewing the results before implementing.

Recent findings suggest that for Ted, the value of ChatGPT Work goes beyond hours saved. Now he can do analysis he might otherwise skip and spend more time on customers, employees, and growing the business.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AI is changing the speed, scale, and economics of cybersecurity.
  • Today, we’re publishing a blueprint for empowering cyber defenders, building on our earlier cybersecurity action strategy and frontier safety blueprint⁠(opens in a new window).
  • Strengthening safety and security for advanced AI: Establish clearer responsibilities for securing frontier models and agents, detecting dangerous behavior, and maintaining reliable shutdown controls for operations under each organization’s control.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, AI is changing the speed, scale, and economics of cybersecurity. It can help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, detect intrusions, and respond to attacks—but those same capabilities can enable malicious actors and create new risks when AI systems act beyond their intended boundaries. We are in a defender’s window: a limited opportunity to put advanced AI into defenders’ hands and strengthen protections before advanced cyber offensive capabilities become widely available.

Today, we’re publishing a blueprint for empowering cyber defenders, building on our earlier cybersecurity action strategy and frontier safety blueprint⁠(opens in a new window). Our experience with misalignment and security incidents involving our own models underscores the need for stronger safeguards and accountability across the industry. Drawing on those lessons, the blueprint puts forward concrete proposals for governments and industry in three areas:.

Strengthening safety and security for advanced AI: Establish clearer responsibilities for securing frontier models and agents, detecting dangerous behavior, and maintaining reliable shutdown controls for operations under each organization’s control.

Modernizing cybersecurity for the intelligence age: Equip defenders with advanced tools, training, and technical support; address longstanding cybersecurity weaknesses; and invest in securing essential services and replacing outdated systems.

Building resilient and adaptive public institutions: Strengthen government evaluations and independent technical assessments, establish consistent incident reporting requirements, and improve coordinated response and recovery.

AI labs have a responsibility to address the risks their systems create and help strengthen society’s defenses. Governments must also have the expertise, resources, and authority to protect the public as capabilities advance. We encourage policymakers to act now—establishing safeguards, learning from experience, and strengthening requirements as the technology evolves.

Read the full blueprint here⁠(opens in a newly introduced window).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Director, State, Local, Higher Ed Central, Google Public Sector.
  • In a recent development, as state and local agencies modernize to meet evolving public needs, leaders have an unprecedented opportunity to empower and elevate their teams.
  • Recent findings suggest that modernizing an agency workforce means transitioning employees from institutional systems to agentic platforms—redirecting their efforts away from manual administration and freeing up time for high-touch service delivery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Director, State, Local, Higher Ed Central, Google Public Sector.

In a recent development, as state and local agencies modernize to meet evolving public needs, leaders have an unprecedented opportunity to empower and elevate their teams. Modernizing public sector operations starts with giving dedicated public servants the right tools to thrive. By replacing repetitive administrative routines with intuitive, intelligent workflows, agencies can free their staff to do what they do best: focus on high-impact problem-solving, build rewarding careers, and deliver responsive, compassionate services to the residents and communities they serve.

Recent findings suggest that modernizing an agency workforce means transitioning employees from institutional systems to agentic platforms—redirecting their efforts away from manual administration and freeing up time for high-touch service delivery. By leveraging Google Cloud’s integrated stack to modernize daily operations, agency leaders can reliably meet regulatory requirements while creating the operational capacity to innovate, develop staff, and strengthen public trust.

Under the leadership of CIO Ted Ross, the City of Los Angeles addressed administrative constraints by deploying Google Workspace with Gemini across its entire 27,500-person municipal workforce. City employees now use agents to instantly synthesize large amounts of grant documents buried in silos and quickly rewrite public web copy for clearer readability. This digital companion allows city staff to step away from time-consuming administrative tasks and spend more time focusing on critical community service delivery, ensuring the city is operationally ready to host major global events like the 2028 Olympics and 2028 Paralympics.

The University of Hawaii needed a better way to keep local talent from leaving the islands. To build and retain regional talent, the university turned to BigQuery and Gemini—creating an automated, skills-first platform that helps match individuals with career opportunities. This solution maps student and faculty capabilities, matches individuals to academic roles and public research projects, and helps retain top talent.

The Indiana Department of Transportation was issued an urgent executive mandate requiring a comprehensive review of complex legal contracts within a strict 30-day window. The agency deployed Gemini to securely ingest, parse, and analyze the state’s contract repositories. The automated system successfully isolated key legal parameters, saving 360 hours of highly skilled engineering labor and meeting the strict deadline.

A similar transformation occurred within Maryland’s state agencies, where caseworkers navigating complex public benefits documentation spent hours indexing files and searching manual handbooks to find specific clause requirements. Maryland deployed Gemini and Gemini Notebook across its 40,000-person state workforce, establishing a secure framework to index and interact with state benefits compliance manuals. Caseworkers can now run plain-language queries to retrieve policy directives in seconds, drastically reducing the administrative processing times for residents.

Giving the public sector workforce a secure starting point for enterprise workflows streamlines routine processes, creating the space for employees to expand their skills and lead strategic mission priorities.
